title: A hurricane releases 200 times the world's electricity
description: From the International Space Station, astronauts witness the immense power and scale of hurricanes. These massive storms release heat at a rate far exceeding global electricity generation.

shots.narration: From orbit, a hurricane appears as a vast spiral with a calm center known as the eye.
This quiet eye is typically thirty to sixty-five kilometres wide, surrounded by a wall of clouds.
The strongest winds blow in this eyewall, reaching speeds that exceed two hundred fifty kilometres per hour.
A large hurricane can be more than one thousand kilometres across, stretching toward the Earth's horizon.
The International Space Station travels so fast that it crosses this entire storm in about two minutes.
North of the equator, these clouds spin anticlockwise, while storms in the southern hemisphere spin clockwise.
A mature hurricane releases heat at a rate about two hundred times the world's electricity generation.
GOES weather satellites watch from thirty-five thousand eight hundred kilometres up to monitor the storm's progress.
These satellites can image a storm every thirty seconds, tracking the eyewall as it moves.
